title: Plan and co-ordinate conservation removal operations

lessons.title: Why and when animals are removed from a conservation area
lessons.html:
Removal as a management tool

On game farms, private reserves and protected areas, animal numbers can grow beyond what the veld can carry. Too many grazers and browsers cause overgrazing, bush encroachment, erosion, loss of plant species and eventually animal die-offs in drought. Removal operations, either live capture for sale or translocation, or culling (humane killing for meat and products), keep populations in line with holistic management objectives.

Basing the decision on evidence

  • Veld condition and carrying capacity: veld condition assessments, rainfall records and grazing and browsing capacity estimates show how many large stock units (or browser units) the area can support.
  • Game counts: aerial or road-strip counts, with trends over several years, show current numbers and herd structure.
  • Population structure: sex ratio and age classes indicate which animals to remove. Removing surplus adult males or old animals has different effects from removing breeding females.
  • Management objectives: tourism viewing, trophy hunting, breeding of rare species, venison production or habitat recovery each lead to different removal targets.
  • Economics: live sale prices versus carcass value and operation costs in ZAR.

Ethical considerations

A culling operation must be justified by sound management reasons, never by convenience alone. The principles are: minimise suffering and stress, use the most humane method suited to the species and terrain, avoid disrupting breeding and dependent young unnecessarily, use the products fully and responsibly, and be open with staff, neighbours and authorities about why it is done.

Legal requirements

Wild animals are protected by national and provincial legislation, including the National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004 and provincial nature conservation ordinances. Removal usually needs permits from the provincial conservation authority, and threatened or protected species have extra requirements. Firearm users must be licensed and competent under the Firearms Control Act 60 of 2000. Meat for sale must go through a registered abattoir or approved game-handling system under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. Always check current permit conditions with the authority before planning; do not rely on what was allowed last year.

lessons.title: Choosing the technique and preparing the operation
lessons.html:
Matching method to species, terrain and objective

TechniqueTypical useMain considerations
Night shooting from a vehicle with a spotlightMedium antelope such as impala or springbok on open terrainSkilled marksmen, head or neck shots, good access roads, carcasses chilled quickly
Helicopter shootingLarger numbers, difficult terrainHigh cost, experienced pilot and shooter, ground teams to recover carcasses
Boma captureLive removal of herd animals, often driven by helicopterFunnel and boma design, plastic or cloth walls, minimal stress, vet support
Drop netsLive capture of species that come to bait or waterBait training, quick release, trained ground crew
Chemical immobilisationIndividual large or valuable animalsOnly by or under a veterinarian, scheduled drugs, darting skill

Planning checklist

  1. Confirm removal numbers by species, sex and age from the management plan.
  2. Obtain permits and notify neighbours, the vet and, for meat, the abattoir or game-handling facility.
  3. Choose the time: cool months reduce meat spoilage and capture stress; avoid late pregnancy and lambing or calving peaks.
  4. Appoint the team: operation leader, marksmen or capture team, drivers, skinners and hygiene staff, data recorder, first aider.
  5. Prepare equipment: calibrated firearms, ammunition suitable for the species, vehicles, lights, radios, slaughter or field-dressing equipment, cold room or refrigerated truck, PPE.
  6. Plan routes, shooting blocks or capture sites and safe zones, and brief everyone in writing.

Safety

  • Hold a safety briefing: firearm handling rules, safe angles of fire, never shooting towards roads, buildings or other teams, radio procedures.
  • Never allow anyone under the influence of alcohol or drugs on the operation.
  • Have a first aid kit, trained first aider and an emergency evacuation plan with the nearest hospital and helicopter contacts.
  • Brief staff on handling wounded or live animals; no one approaches a downed animal until the marksman confirms it is dead.

lessons.title: Carrying out the operation and collecting scientific data
lessons.html:
During the operation

The operation leader controls the work, keeps radio contact with all teams and can stop the operation at any time for safety, weather or welfare reasons. Marksmen take only clean, certain shots; a wounded animal must be followed up and dispatched immediately, which is the first priority over taking more animals. Live-capture teams keep noise low, limit chase times and move animals into transport crates or holding bomas quickly under veterinary guidance.

Carcass handling and hygiene

  • Bleed and eviscerate within the time required by the game meat system you use, on clean surfaces.
  • Tag each carcass with a number linked to the data sheet.
  • Keep carcasses off the ground, shaded and out of dust; get them into chilling as fast as possible.
  • Inspect organs for signs of disease and report abnormalities to the vet; do not send suspect carcasses for human consumption.
  • Dispose of offal and waste so that it does not attract problem animals or pollute water.

Supervising the collection of scientific data

A cull is a valuable chance to learn about the population. Agree the data needed with the ecologist or vet beforehand and use standard data sheets.

DataWhy it matters
Species, sex, age class (tooth wear or eruption)Population structure
Body mass, carcass massCondition and yield
Kidney fat index or body condition scoreNutritional status of the veld
Pregnancy and foetus sizeReproduction rates and timing
Parasite load and samplesDisease surveillance
GPS locationDistribution across the area

Check sheets at the end of every session for completeness. Label samples clearly and store and send them as the laboratory instructs.

After the operation

Reconcile numbers removed against the permit and plan, report to the authority as required, record income and costs, debrief the team on safety and welfare and update the management plan with the new data.

Key points

  • Removal decisions must rest on veld condition, game counts, population structure and management objectives.
  • Get permits, notify authorities and neighbours, and use licensed, competent marksmen.
  • Choose the most humane technique for the species, terrain and objective.
  • Following up a wounded animal always comes before taking the next animal.
  • Collect standard scientific data from every animal and use it to update the plan.

options.text: To keep the population in line with carrying capacity and management objectives
Because it is required every year regardless of numbers

Continue shooting to reach the target number
